en: Record of the Transmission of the Dharma between Masters and Disciples in the Two Great Sections of the Law, Part One:
A Record of the Successive Order of the Dharma Transmission in the Two Sections;
a Brief Account by Haiyun of the Successive Order of the Dharma Transmission between Masters and Disciples in the *Vajradhātu-mahātantrarāja-sūtra*.
Record. Tripitaka Master Vajrabodhi said:
"I have come from the Kingdom of Southern India."
The Master personally received this *Vajradhātu-lakṣa-grantha* from the Ācārya Nāgabodhi, who himself declared:
Vairocana Tathāgata is none other than Śākyamuni Tathāgata; this is designated as being in the world in reference to the Dharma-nature body (dharmatākāya).
By means of this Vajradhātu Mahāyāna vehicle, [he manifests].
It was entrusted to Samantabhadra-vajrasattva;
Samantabhadra-vajrasattva entrusted it to Mañjuśrī-bodhisattva;
and Mañjuśrī-bodhisattva transmitted it through twelve successive generations.
He entrusted the Dharma to the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna—Nāgārjuna being the same as Ārya Nāgārjuna.

Because this Bodhisattva was born beneath a dragon-tree (nāga-vṛkṣa), he was named Nāgārjuna. After several hundred years, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna further entrusted the Dharma to the Ācārya Nāgabodhi.
After another hundred-odd years, these two holy masters achieved the fruits of the Path;

both lived for several hundred years and transmitted the Dharma to the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi—whose name in Sanskrit is *Vajra-gīyana* and who is translated here as "Vajra-Wisdom. The Tripiṭaka Master Upādhyāya Vajrabodhi was a master of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings.
He followed the Sarvāstivāda school;
his observance of the precepts was frost-like in its purity,
and he took the Vinaya as his guiding standard.
The third son of the King of South India, for the sake of propagating the Dharma, traveled with his staff through the five regions of India and came to visit China.
At that time, there was a Tripitaka Master from the country of Central India.
By birth he belonged to the Śākya clan;

he was the fifty-second descendant of King Droṇodana. Because his father the king had been dispatched on a mission of war, he subsequently witnessed the mass slaughter and cruel atrocities committed therein.
Consequently, he took no pleasure in the royal throne;
weary of the world, he left the household life and vowed to transmit the Dharma to the Eastern Land.
Together with the Tripitaka Master Vajrabodhi,
he served as a National Preceptor during the Xuanzong reign. Knowing that the Tripitaka Master possessed profound wisdom regarding the Vajradhātu-dharma,
he subsequently requested from the Tripitaka Master Vajrabodhi the transmission of the five families of the Vajradhātu teachings.
At that time, the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi, knowing that the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi of Central India understood the teachings of the Great Vairocana, exclaimed:
"This Dharma is most profound; it is difficult to encounter and difficult to meet. In the past, while in South India, I heard of the existence of the teachings of the Great Vairocana."
He subsequently traveled through the Five Indias seeking [this teaching], but found no one who could explain it.
Now, having arrived in the Great Tang, he joyfully encountered this doctrine;
he then invited the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi to request the transmission of the Great Teaching of Mahāvairocana.
Jian transmitted the two versions of the teachings through the lineage of master and disciple.
Furthermore, the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi entrusted this King of Tantras of the Vajradhātu to the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra of Daxingshan Temple.

The Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra further entrusted this Dharma to five disciples, including the Ācārya Hanguang. First, the Ācārya Hanguang was commanded by an imperial edict from Emperor Daizong to repair the Northern Wutai Mountains and construct Jinguesi Monastery;

being occupied with these tasks, he did not have leisure to transmit the Dharma. Second, the Ācārya Huilang of Daxingshan Monastery transmitted it to the Indian Ācārya at Chongfu Monastery. The Indian Ācārya transmitted it to the layman Zhao Jiu (of the surnames Demei and Huijin). Third, the Ācārya Tanzheng of Qinglong Monastery did not transmit it to any disciple; whenever there were those who wished to study the Dharma, he would say, "At Dongta Monastery, there is the Ācārya Huiguo, who is well-versed in the teachings and their characteristics; you may study there. Fourth, the Ācārya Juechao of Baoshou Monastery transmitted it to Qiru.
The Acharya Hui-de of the East Pagoda Cloister at Gyeongboksa Temple was Hui-guo Acharya, who was well-versed in the science of phonetics and was proficient in both Chinese and Sanskrit.
He constantly dwelt his mind within the gateway of the true nature of reality (dharmatā).
He attained a wondrous realization of the principle of suchness (tathatā) and constantly recited the Vimalakīrti Sūtra;
furthermore, during his leisure time, he regularly perused it.
Nirvana, Avatamsaka, Prajñāpāramitā.
At Laṅkā and Siyi,
he further encountered the Tripiṭaka Master Daxingshan, who transmitted to him the Vajradhātu.
He then said, "This teaching is most supreme and most wondrous.
Nevertheless, the Mahayana Mind-Ground (Cittabhūmi) realized in the past was also ultimate and most wondrous.
Now, having encountered the Vajradhātu Dharma-gate..."
It is even more supreme;
thus it is said to be "ultimately unsurpassed.
Furthermore, the Mind-Ground (Cittabhūmi) of the Exoteric Teachings clarifies only the contemplation of principle (li-guan).
Now, this Yoga teaching encompasses both the gates of principle and phenomena;
abiding within the Vajradhātu,
one attains correspondence in a single thought-moment.
He then attained perfect enlightenment;
therefore, it is said that there is nothing superior to this.
As for the Vajradhātu Dharma transmitted [therein]:
There were also Acharya Huiying and Huitze, who studied the teachings of the consecration (abhiṣeka) at Daxingshan Temple; as well as Weishang of Chengdu Prefecture, and Bianhong of Bianlin.
The monk Hye-il of Silla, the monk Kūkai of Japan,
and Ui-mun of Qinglong Monastery.
Yiming, Yicao, and Yizhao.
Yimǐn, Yìzhèng, and Yìyī.

The fourteen individuals above, beginning with the lay practitioner (upāsaka) Yinyin, all transmitted the Great Teaching; they followed in the rank of the successive *ācāryas* and were those who received the transmission from *Ācārya* Yicao of the East Pagoda Cloister at Qinglong Temple.
Regarding the Great Dharma of the Vajradhātu,
there was a fellow practitioner at this very temple named Faron.
Yijeong, Yijung, and Uigwon.
The monk Shen-da of Jinggong Temple;
the monk Hai-yun of Jingzhu Temple;
and the monk Da-yu of Chongfu Temple.
Sengcong of Liquan Temple; Wen Yuan;
and Jue Liang, a monk from the kingdom of Silla at Huichang Temple.
At this monastery, Changjian and the monks Zhi-shen and Fa-quan of Xuanfasi [were present].

The fourteen disciples, including Sengwen and Bibi, have all received the Great Dharma of the Vajradhātu; as they have each attained the rank of Ācārya in succession, they have obtained the Great Teachings of the Vajradhātu.
It has spread throughout the world,
its branches and leaves never ceasing;
such is the teaching of the Udumbara flower.
The full syllables are now perfected.
Those who receive the transmission of the Vajradhātu Dharma will suddenly behold Bodhi.
He enters the maṇḍala and receives the ācārya consecration,
just as one is invested with the rank of a Dharma-wheel-turning king.
This Great King of Teachings is named *Vajradhātu*.
"Vajra" signifies the meaning of "solidity.
It symbolizes the fact that the *dharmakāya* of all Tathāgatas is solid, indestructible, unborn and unceasing, without beginning or end, eternally existing, and imperishable.
The "element" (*dhātu*) refers to the fundamental nature.

It clarifies that the nature of the Vajra of all Tathāgatas pervades all bodies possessing perception, being primordially endowed with the ocean-like nature and merit of the self-nature body of Samantabhadra-Vairocana’s great function.

Therefore, the practitioner of yoga further employs the samādhi of the Great Bliss Samantabhadra Vajra-Arrow to destroy the seeds and manifestations of the two obstacles residing in the ground of ignorance, as well as the seeds of the two vehicles.
Crushing them without remainder,
one realizes the state of Mahāvairocana in a single thought-moment.
This sutra is also titled the *Vajraśekhara*.
Just as the crown of a person's head is the most supreme part of the body,
so too this teaching is the most honored and exalted among all Mahāyāna teachings.

Therefore, it is named *Vajraśekhara* (in Sanskrit: *Vajraśekhara*; in Chinese: *Jingangding*). It is also the Vairocana of the Vajradhātu, the Tathāgata who manifests the body of perfect enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*), revealing the three mysteries and five wisdoms to cause all sentient beings to realize the Great Mirror-like Wisdom and attain Great Bodhi.
The Sanskrit original of this sutra consists of one hundred thousand verses.
The abbreviated version contains four thousand verses,
while the extensive version comprises an infinite number of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of atoms of dust in its verses.
As stated in the *Vajraśekhara-artha-nirṇaya*,
there is a great iron stūpa in the country of South India,
within which is the Vajradhātu Maṇḍala.
The image of the Noble One was cast from iron;
within that stupa were Sanskrit scriptures as wide as a bed.
It was eight or nine feet wide and five or six feet high, consisting entirely of the *Vajradhātu-mahātantrarāja-vistara* in its extensive Sanskrit version.

From this, one knows that the extensive version of this sutra contains verses numbering as many as immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of atoms; it cannot be measured by an ordinary mind. As the "Parable of the Phantom City" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "This *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* consists of verses as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
Furthermore, the "Bhaiṣajyarāja-pūrvayoga-parivarta" speaks in verses of the Khaṅgila, Vibhāṣā, Akṣobhya, and others; thus,
the teaching is expounded according to the faculties [of beings], varying in its breadth and brevity.
This is just as in the three versions of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
the upper version contains verses numbering as many as the atoms in thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms,
and chapters numbering as many as the atoms in the four continents.

The medium-length version consists of as many verses as there are atoms in the four continents; the third version consists of one hundred thousand verses, which is precisely the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in eighty fascicles and so forth. This is just like the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra*, where the abbreviated Sanskrit manuscript contains four thousand verses and the medium-length version contains one hundred thousand verses.

The extensive version consists of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis of nayutas of gāthās; furthermore, as stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, it has as its retinue sūtras as numerous as the atoms within a buddha-field.
Formerly, during the Yao Qin period, the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva brought this *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and declared it to be the original version of the Bodhisattva Precepts Sūtra.
It was translated in brief as two fascicles;
it is said to represent the shallow and abbreviated aspects within this sutra.
Furthermore, during the Kaiyuan era of the Great Tang, the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi brought from South India a Sanskrit manuscript of the *Vajradhātu* consisting of one hundred thousand verses.
At that time, amidst a great and violent storm upon the vast ocean,
all the treasures, the relics, and the merit within the three ships were cast into the sea;
likewise, the one hundred thousand verses of the Brahma-scripture were also mistakenly lost and cast into the sea.
At that time, Tripitaka performed the rite for pacifying calamities,
whereupon the wind finally ceased.
Thus we know that because the connection between this scripture of one hundred thousand verses and the conditions of this land was thin, this King of Sutras sank into the great ocean.

Next, during the ninth year of the Tiānbǎo era of the Great Táng dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra traveled in person to the Five Indias to seek out the most excellent teachings; while on his journey, he encountered the long-lived Ācārya Samantabhadra in the kingdom of South India.
He then requested instruction once more to relearn the Vajradhātu-dharma.

Because he was about to obtain the *Daśasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, certain aspects of the Vajradhātu teachings he had previously studied were slightly different; thus, the Tripiṭaka Master of Daxingshan Temple became the Abhiṣeka Master for Emperor Daizong.
He frequently expounded the profound meanings and flavors of the Vajradhātu with the Emperor.
He constantly translated the holy teachings within the inner palace chapel.
Among his disciples under his tutelage, there were those who received the empowerment of the Vidyādhara.
The number [of followers] exceeded ten million.
Those who ascended the hall to participate in the translation work numbered more than thirty people.
Those who entered the inner chamber to receive the *ācārya* empowerment were even fewer.

The number [of assemblies] is only five, as already described in the preceding text. The *Vairocana-vajradhātu* in its Sanskrit original consists of one hundred thousand verses—that is, one hundred thousand *gāthās*. Regarding the locations where the sūtra was preached, there are eighteen assemblies; their titles, enumerations, and sequence are as set forth in the *Shibabahui zhiguai* (Exposition of the Eighteen Assemblies). There are four major sections.
First, Vajradhātu;
second, Trailokyavijaya;
third, Sarvārthasiddhi.

Fourth is the accomplishment of all aims. These four types are all subsumed within the Vajradhātu; they are the essential points of all dharmas, which are gathered by the four seals (mudrās), namely: the Great Seal (mahāmudrā), the Samaya Seal (samayamudrā), [the Dharma Seal (dharmamudrā), and the Karma Seal (karmamudrā)].
The Dharma-knowledge seal and the Karma-knowledge seal.
Furthermore, each and every maṇḍala is complete with six maṇḍalas.
First, the so-called Great Maṇḍala;
second, the Samaya Maṇḍala; third, the Dharma Maṇḍala.
4. The Maṇḍala of the Four Karmas;
5. The Maṇḍala of the Five Mudrās;
6. The Maṇḍala of the Single Mudrā.
Only the Trailokyavijaya Maṇḍala possesses ten maṇḍalas;
all others possess six.
The sūtra speaks of five families (pañcakula).
First, in the Buddha Family (Buddhakula), Vairocana Buddha serves as the patriarch of the family,
with the four Bodhisattvas of the Pāramitās as his attendants.
Second, in the Vajra Family (Vajrakula), Akṣobhya Buddha serves as the patriarch of the family, with the four Great Bodhisattvas as his attendants.
In the Ratna Family, Ratnasambhava Buddha serves as the patriarch of the family, with four great bodhisattvas serving as his attendants.
In the Padma Family, Amitābha Buddha serves as the patriarch of the family, with four great bodhisattvas serving as his attendants.
In the Karma-kula (Five Karmic Ritual Section), Amoghasiddhi Buddha serves as the presiding lord, with four great bodhisattvas as his attendants.
Through internal and external offerings and the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), these constitute thirty-seven [deities].
Furthermore, four kinds of dharmakāya are taught:
first, the svabhāvakāya;
second, the sambhogakāya.
Third, the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya);
fourth, the body of natural outflow (niṣyandakāya).
These are the four stages of the grounds.
1. The stage of practice through resolute belief;
2. The stage of Samantabhadra’s conduct and vows;
3. The great stage of Samantabhadra.
The fourth is the Stage of Universal Radiance (*samantaprabhā-bhūmi*).
The three stages of the worthy ones prior to the [first] ground constitute the Stage of Practice through Resolute Conviction (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).
From the first ground through the tenth ground constitutes the Stage of the Vows and Conduct of Samantabhadra (*samantabhadracaryāpraṇidhāna-bhūmi*).
The Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment is the stage of Great Samantabhadra;
the Buddha is named the Stage of Universal Radiance.
There are four kinds of recitation.
1. Recitation with a single sound;

2. Recitation with two words, also called vajra-recitation, which consists of slightly moving the tip of the tongue while the lips and teeth remain closed; and 3. samādhi-recitation, which consists of abiding in meditative concentration in conjunction with the wisdom of insight (vipaśyanā).
The fourth is the recitation of the ultimate meaning, which contemplates the principle of the ultimate truth as it has long been.
The four types of ritual methods for making petitions—namely, pacifying, increasing, subjugating, and magnetizing—along with summoning, constitute five.
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* elucidates four kinds of eyes as explained in the sūtras;
four kinds of seats as explained in the sūtras;
and five kinds of great vows as explained in the sūtras.
Furthermore, within the *Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha-yoga*, one hundred and twenty types of homa hearths are taught.
The mudrās and insignia held within these hearths each differ,
and they swiftly accomplish the desired mundane and supramundane fruits.

In the vast and expansive assembly, the central maṇḍala features thirty-seven honored positions, along with sixteen great bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, representing the one thousand buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa;
alternatively, all one thousand buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa [are represented].
In the four directions of the maṇḍala,
surrounding the great maṇḍala,
there are fifty-three [deities].
Together with the twenty deities of the outer perimeter, this constitutes seventy-three.
The inner courtyard, consisting of the earth, water, fire, and wind elements, constitutes seventy-seven.
At the four corners are the four wrathful vidyārājas, or their symbolic emblems, forming eighty-one sacred bodies in total.

The above are collectively named the fifty-three holy beings belonging to the consecration deities within the Vajradhātu Great Maṇḍala King; the remaining deities all belong to the outer Vajra Family and do not enter the stage of consecration. Including the Vajradhātu Maṇḍala and the deities of the outer Vajra Family, there are eighty-one in total.
These are all the manifestations of the Tathāgata Vairocana of the Vajradhātu,

representing the bodies of all Tathāgatas throughout the oceans of lands as numerous as atoms, pervading the entirety of space and the Dharma-realm across the ten directions and the three periods of time.
He considered that this essence is also the Mother Prajñāpāramitā of all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods of time,
who is fully capable of giving birth to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Vajrasattvas, and those Bodhisattvas accomplished through their inherent nature.
It can also transcend the world, [revealing] the hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sūtra-piṭakas of profound secrets;

all are the meritorious qualities of the ocean of the nature of the Tathāgata Vairocana. It can also transcend the world, [revealing] the sentient-being world and the vessel-world within the Flower Treasury Adorned World-Ocean.
Because the essence of Vairocana Tathāgata pervades everywhere, his single body fills all lands;
therefore, it is said that this teaching is difficult to encounter and difficult to meet.
Therefore, those who transmitted the Dharma from above have passed down the teachings for several hundred years;
yet in foreign lands, it has been transmitted by only a single person.
Our own Tripiṭaka Master of Daxingshan Temple personally paid homage in the Five Indias.
He again consulted on the supreme Dharma,
and its teachings spread throughout the world;
thus the Great Dharma flourished and was widely propagated.
Therefore, the various kingdoms of Silla have traveled tens of thousands of li,
braving the perils of the sea and disregarding their own lives,
to come and seek refuge in our Great Tang.
In order to seek the supreme Dharma,
he obtained imperial edicts for each successive year to maintain [the transmission] at Daxingshan Temple,
Qinglong Temple, Baoshou Temple, Xingtang Temple, Chongfu Temple, and Nongquan Temple.
They extensively conferred the empowerment and transmitted the Dharma to save sentient beings;

all of these were the descendants of the lineage of the Dharma-transmission of the Tripiṭaka Master of our Great Xingshan Monastery, who propagated the teachings as successive branches that mutually upheld and maintained them.
It is eternal and inexhaustible.
During a moment of leisure, the Bhikṣu Sāgaramegha,
at a time belonging to the month of mid-autumn, [composed this].
I have respectfully compiled, based on our own tradition, a concise account of the successive transmission of the Dharma from master to disciple within the Great King of Teachings of the Vajradhātu,
which has been passed down from Samantabhadra-Vajrasattva to the present day through the Eight Petals.
Homage to the Sovereign of the Vajradhātu,
Samantabhadra-sattva, the King of Vidyādharas.
May the merit from this recitation of praise be dedicated for the benefit of all sentient beings.
May all universally aspire to be born together in the Flower Treasury Realm (*Huāzàngjiè*).

Compiled on the twentieth day of the middle month of autumn in the eighth year of the Dàhé era of the Great Táng (the year of Jiǎyín), by the Śramaṇa Hǎiyún, a transmitter of the teachings in Sanskrit at Jìngzhù Temple, from the *Jìlǎngbù dàfǎ xiāngchéng shīzī fùfǎ jì* (Record of the Transmission of the Dharma between Masters and Disciples Concerning the Two Great Dharma Sections). Part II.
A Brief Account of the Transmission of the *Mahāvairocana-buddhotpatti-adhiṣṭhāna-vaipulya-sūtra*:

A Record of the Successive Stages of the Entrustment of the Great Teaching. The title of the scripture is the *Mahāvairocana-buddhotpatti-adhiṣṭhāna-sūtra*. In Sanskrit it is called *Mahā*; this is translated as "Great.

*Vairocana* is translated as "Universal Radiance" or "Great Sun Universal Radiance. The correct Sanskrit term should be *Vairocana* (with the first syllable pronounced as *ve* with the *u* vowel and the second syllable as *lu* with the *o* vowel). *Vairocana* is an archaic translation.
According to the interpretation in the *Vajraśekhara-artha-nirṇaya*,
this Vairocana is translated as the Tathāgata of the Infinite and Vast Eye-Cluster;
"eye" refers to wisdom (*jñāna*).
It is said that this Dharmakāya Tathāgata’s wisdom and ten eyes are without limit;

his divine power, wisdom, and myriad virtues are already perfected, being as boundless in measure as the realm of empty space and exceeding all numerical calculation. Alternatively, it is called the *Vairocana-buddhatva-sūtra*.

In Sanskrit it is called *Vairocana-samudra-vyūha-sūtra*, which in Chinese means "The Sūtra of the Venerable Universal Illumination Mahāvairocana. There are three versions of this sūtra in Sanskrit manuscripts.
The extensive version consists of one hundred thousand verses;
if translated in its entirety according to the Sanskrit original, it would comprise approximately three hundred fascicles.
This extensive version exists in the Western Regions but has not reached this land.
The abbreviated version of the Brahma-sūtra consists of four thousand verses;
there is also another abbreviated version consisting of two thousand five hundred verses.
Compiled by a Great Ācārya of Central India, this work currently transmitted consists of four thousand verses.
The Śākya śramaṇa Tripiṭaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha translated it by imperial decree in the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era.
The śramaṇa Yixing acted as the scribe;
this is precisely the *Mahāvairocana-buddhābhisaṃbodhi-vikurvāṇādhiṣṭhāna-sūtra*.
It is said that this sutra is sustained by the miraculous transformations and spiritual empowerments (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata Vairocana.
Based on the Sanskrit manuscript,
this was translated into six fascicles.
Furthermore, a single volume was compiled containing the general collection of the sequence for the recitation and retention of the teachings.
It consists of seven fascicles,
forming one complete work,
and has been included in the Tripitaka.
At that time, the Tathāgata Vairocana was in the Vajra-Dharmadhātu Palace,

together with Samantabhadra and other great Bodhisattvas numbering as many as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields, as well as Vajrapāṇi Guhyakas numbering as many as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields, and the world-protecting lords of the gods and other Vajradharas numbering as many as the atoms in ten Buddha-fields.
Their number is immeasurable and beyond description;
they are all sustained by the empowerment of the vast Dharma-realm of the ocean-like self-enjoyment body of Vairocana Tathāgata.
The Sūtra clarifies that a Bodhisattva who practices the words and deeds of cultivation trains in the unsurpassed bodhicitta,
transcends one hundred and sixty types of forgetful minds,
and abides in the great bodhicitta.
Through a single thought-moment of correspondence, one traverses three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;
at the very moment of first generating the mind, one attains the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
This sutra relies upon two kinds of practice.
The bodhicitta is the cause;
great compassion is the root; skillful means is the culmination.
Next, the ten phrases on dependent origination are explained.
This refers to the Bodhisattva who clearly cultivates the practices of mantra and conduct, understanding that all phenomena are like illusions, arising from conditions.
Furthermore, this is based on the two truths—the ultimate and the conventional.
If one relies upon the ultimate truth:
One practices to establish the maṇḍala of the dharmakāya.
For this reason, this sūtra states that one first visualizes the maṇḍala within empty space.
Therefore, the dharmakāya of the tutelary deity is free from form and color, just like empty space.
Abiding in this samādhi, if one practices according to the conventional truth by relying on the four wheels as a maṇḍala:

if the noble deity is yellow, he abides in the earth-wheel maṇḍala, which is square in shape and is called the "Noble Golden Wheel"; if the noble deity is white, he abides in the water-wheel maṇḍala, which is circular in shape and is called the "Noble Water Wheel"; if the noble deity is red, he abides in the fire-wheel maṇḍala, which is triangular in shape; and if the noble deity is blue or black, he abides in the wind-wheel maṇḍala, which is shaped like a half-moon. The great maṇḍala is established upon the pedestal of an eight-petaled lotus.
The five Buddhas and four Bodhisattvas are installed within the center and petals of the platform.
Outside the maṇḍala,
there are furthermore three types of maṇḍalas.
1. The maṇḍala of all Tathāgatas; 2. The maṇḍala of Śākyamuni; 3. The maṇḍala of Mañjuśrī.
This is collectively named the Great Compassion Womb Matrix Maṇḍala.
Regarding the method for the disciple’s reception of empowerment, this minor maṇḍala is extremely subtle and detailed, such that it cannot be substituted by other sections [of the ritual].
In this context, the practice of making offerings incorporates two types:
the ritual (vastu) and the principle (nyāya).
Within this sūtra, one hundred and twenty-five kinds of homa hearths are described.
There are forty-four types of homa fire deities;
among them, twelve types of fire are the most excellent.
Within those, there are five types of wisdom fires that are supremely sublime.
These serve as the initial forms for the hearth;
furthermore, wood with milky sap and bitter *gālava* are used differently according to their purpose.
The aspirations of those in the east, south, west, and north each differ.
The internal and external homas likewise rely on the five wheels to seek the four kinds of matters.
Swift accomplishment;
pacification, enrichment,
subjugation, and magnetizing.
That is to say, the fire deities are each different:
some are tranquil and serene,
while others are wrathful.
One should sequentially understand joy and anger,
as well as the modes of practice based on the suffering taught in the extensive scriptures.
It is extremely vast.
For now, I shall briefly set forth a small portion of the purport of the *Mahāvairocana-mahātantrarāja-sūtra*.
Following that, I shall clarify the sequence of the transmission of the Dharma from master to disciple through successive generations.
However, Haiyun feared that the transmission of the Great Teaching between teacher and disciple might be interrupted, causing the Great Dharma to decline and be forgotten over the years.
The Tripiṭaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha said:
"This Dharma originated from Vairocana Buddha."
This was entrusted to the Bodhisattva Vajrapāṇi; after being transmitted for several hundred years, it reached the Ācārya Dharmagupta at Nālandā Monastery in Central India.
The Ācārya Dharmagupta next entrusted [the teaching] to the Tripiṭaka Master Śākyavaṃśa Bhadraśrī (in Sanskrit: Cūḍāmaṇi Saṃgha), who was of the Śākya clan and a native of Central India.

In Chinese he was called Śubhakarasiṃha. A Tripitaka Master who had studied the Five Sciences (pañcavidyāsthāna) and was well-versed in the Three Baskets (tripiṭaka), there were no arts of the Five Indias that he did not master.
He was a descendant in the fifty-second generation of King Droṇodana.
He abdicated the throne in succession and left the household life to enter the Way.
In the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era, he arrived from the Western Regions.
He brought the Mahāvairocana Sūtra and other scriptures to this country.
Emperor Xuanzong honored him as National Preceptor and accompanied him on his travels between the two capitals.
Having translated the *Mahāvairocana* and other sūtras, he became a Great Ācārya for the consecration of the Mahāvairocana Maṇḍala.
Furthermore, the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi took this *Mahāvairocanābhisambodhi-tantra-rāja*.
The Tripitaka Master Vajrabodhi from the Kingdom of India further transmitted the Great King of Teachings of the Vajradhātu to the Tripitaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha;
they served as each other’s ācāryas.
They were transmitted to one another in succession.

As for the Tripitaka Master Vajrabodhi—Vajra-gīyana in Sanskrit, which translates into Chinese as Jīngāngzhì (Vajrabodhi)—the Tripitaka Master was well-versed in both the Mahayana and Hinayana teachings.
He mastered the treatises on grammar (śabda-vidyā) and, within the Sarvāstivāda school,
renounced the world as a son of the king of a kingdom in South India, subsequently relinquishing his royal throne.
Having left the household life to travel to China,
he vowed to propagate the holy teachings.
Emperor Xuanzong honored him as National Preceptor.
Accompanying the imperial entourage to the two capitals,
he translated the *Vajraśekhara-mahātantrarāja* and other scriptures.
As the Vajrācārya for the consecration of the Vajradhātu Maṇḍala, the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi further brought the *Mahāvairocana-mahātantrarāja*.

To the Tripiṭaka Master Amoghavajra (Sanskrit: Amoghasiddhi), also known as Ajñāna (Sanskrit: Amogha-jñāna), Abbot of Daixingshan Monastery, who embodies the five families and the five secret essentials.
Entering the mind that is the ocean of the nature of Samantabhadra,
one who abides in yoga immediately enters the Buddha Vehicle and expounds the mantras.
Thus, the celestial Māras were crushed and destroyed.
From the reigns of Emperor Xuanzong, Suzong, to Daizong, the imperial envoys prostrated themselves at the three courts;
their hearts held him in precious veneration, honoring him as they would a Buddha.
Emperor Daizong invited him to serve as the Great Ācārya for the Consecration (Abhiṣeka).
He transmitted the Great Teachings for over forty years and translated a total of more than one hundred scriptures and treatises.
The Tripiṭaka Master of Daxingshan Monastery received the Vajradhātu-dharma from the Great Master, the Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi;
yet, he further feared that the Great Teaching was not yet complete.
He traveled in person to the kingdom of South India,
where he personally paid homage to the long-lived Ācārya Samantabhadra and once again received the teachings on the *Vajradhātu-pañcakula-śatasahasra-gāthā-dharma*.

Because these two volumes of the Great King of Teachings (*Mahātantrarāja*), which comprise one hundred thousand verses, are secret, profound, and difficult to encounter, they have been transmitted to but a few worthy recipients.
Only after several centuries has it been passed down to a single individual. Since the Buddha-dharma first spread to the eastern land of China, nearly one thousand years have elapsed.

All the secret Mind-Ground teachings currently in circulation do not exceed these two great Kings of Teachings: namely, the Great King of Teachings of Mahāvairocana and the Great King of Teachings of the Vajradhātu.

Following the teachings on the practice of *dhāraṇī* that encompass all [methods], there is next the Susiddhi, here translated as the "Teaching of Sublime Accomplishment," which extensively elucidates the three families (*trikula*) and likewise subsumes the treatises on the methods of *dhāraṇī* practice.
In this context, the explanation of the accomplishment of the ritual action (*karmasiddhi*) is interrelated in meaning with the Vajradhātu and Mahāvairocana;
it is also an extremely essential and subtle teaching.
The translations by the Tripiṭaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha, together with the two aforementioned Mahāyāna teachings and the Susiddhi, constitute the three-part Mahāyāna teachings.
These were subsequently translated and disseminated by the Tripiṭaka Upādhyāya at Daxingshan Temple.

At that time, the Tripitaka Master Śubhakarasiṃha further transmitted this Great King of Teachings of Mahāvairocana to the śramaṇa Yixing of Daxingshan Temple and the śramaṇa Xuanchao of Baoshou Temple from Silla.

Once the śramaṇa Ichigyō had finished transmitting the teachings, he composed the *Mahāvairocana-artha-śāstra* (Great Vairocana Treatise on Meaning) in seven fascicles, which was later expanded into fourteen fascicles; he also produced an abridged translation in two fascicles.
Furthermore, he compiled one fascicle titled *Mahāvairocana-bimba-ākṛti-maṇḍala-vidhi* (Diagram of the Mahāvairocana Image and Maṇḍala Ritual).
*The Ritual for the Mandala of the Banner and Emblem*, one fascicle;
*The Method of Mudrās and Seals*, one fascicle;
*The Decisions on the Meaning of the Vajraśekhara Sūtra*, three fascicles (the upper fascicle exists).
The remaining two fascicles were missing from the original manuscript. Master Yi Xing of Daxing Tangsi was bold and daring in his mastery of astronomy;

he was thoroughly versed in both internal (Buddhist) and external (secular) learning, and there were none of the Chinese or Sanskrit scriptures and histories that he did not penetrate and understand clearly.
Whenever he accompanied Emperor Xuanzong at court audiences or participated in the translation of scriptures, he had no leisure to transmit the Dharma.
Subsequently, the śramaṇa Ācārya Xuanchao further transmitted the Mahāvairocana Great King of Teachings and the Susiddhi teachings to the East Pagoda of Qinglong Monastery.
The preceptor Enkō of the Monastery further transmitted [the teachings] to the monk Wuishang of Chengdu Prefecture— also known as Weiming— and to Bianhong of Bianzhou,
as well as to the Silla monk Hyeil.
Wuzhen. Kūkai of Japan. The monk Yiman of this temple.
Clarifying the meaning;
verifying the meaning;
illuminating the meaning.
Yi Cao, Yi Min, and Fa Run—

those who were conferred the rank of *ācārya* through the Dharma-transmission empowerment numbered one hundred and twelve. Some remained in the capital to maintain the transmission, while others propagated the teachings in various regions outside.
Many of them subsequently perished; next, the Acharya Yicao of the East Pagoda Monastery transmitted [the teachings] to his fellow student, the monk Yizhen;
then to Shen Da of Jinggong Temple;
and finally to Haiyun, a disciple of Jingzhu Temple.
The monk Daeyu of Chongbok-sa and Munwon of Gyijeon-sa—
these five persons above were all Ajāryas in the lineage of transmission for the propagation of the teachings.
Next, Ajārya Narun of Dongta-yeon transmitted them to the monk Doseung of Jeongbeop-sa.
Humble submission of Faquan of Xuánfǎ Monastery.
This *Mahāvairocana-mahātantrarāja*, also known as the *Mahākaruṇā-garbha-vairocana*, originates from the fundamental great compassion of the Tathāgata.
The arising of the great bodhicitta, the accomplishment of bodhisattva conduct from that bodhicitta,
the subsequent realization of great enlightenment and nirvāṇa,
and the attainment of the body of the five wisdoms through the perfection of skillful means— all these proceed from this.

Because it is the gateway of the letter "Dha" (the long vowel), which signifies the prolongation of evil, the Sūtra states that skillful means constitute the ultimate goal and are able to accomplish all the works of the Buddhas.
This is like a Wheel-Turning Sage King who, when about to take birth, entrusts himself to the womb of a noble queen.
One should know that the Holy King will soon be born.
When a practitioner of yoga gives rise to the bodhicitta and dwells in the contemplation of the letter A,
observing the non-arising of all phenomena, this is precisely dwelling within the womb of Vairocana.
As stated in the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* of the Exoteric Mahāyāna:

"The thirty individuals of the Holy Embryo of Submissive Patience—namely, the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), and the ten transferences (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*)—are called the thirty minds prior to the stages (*bhūmi-pūrva-triṃśac-citta*)."
This is called "dwelling in the noble womb.
This refers to the practice prior to the stages of a Bodhisattva in the Gradual Enlightenment of the Exoteric Teachings,
lasting for one great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*.
At this point, one is first named a Bodhisattva dwelling in the noble womb (*āryagarbha*).
This is not the case for a Bodhisattva who practices the true words and deeds as an external ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*).
In a single moment of thought, they become fully endowed with the body of the five wisdoms (*pañcajñānakāya*).
One abides in the state of the Great Vairocana Buddha;
with the entire dharma-realm as the surrounding gallery, it constitutes the essence of the maṇḍala. Merely abiding in this mind is called "entering the holy embryo" (garbha).
When contemplation reaches its ultimate consummation, it is called "attaining the stage of Buddhahood."
This is called transcending three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* to realize *bodhi*.
Above, I have fully elucidated the intent of the teachings of the *Guhya-garbha-tantra*.
Now, relying respectfully upon both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings, I shall briefly set forth their origins.
The intent of the teaching is profound and vast, its depths difficult to fathom;
yet I, Haiyun, having received the Buddha’s protection by grace, have been fortunate enough to encounter this supreme instruction.
Having personally inherited the Eye of the Dharma,
it has been transmitted from the Great Vairocana Susiddhi down through the lineage to the present seventh generation;
herein I briefly describe its essential tenets.

In accordance with what has been seen and heard, I have briefly recorded this sequence; may all those possessed of wisdom kindly provide instruction. I prostrate to the Omniscient One of the three periods of time, Samantabhadra, Guhyadhara, and Vajradhara.
May the merit from this recitation of praise be dedicated to all sentient beings, and may they all be born together in the Land of Peace and Bliss.

Recorded on the eighth day of the first ten-day period of the month of Jia-Yin in the eighth year of the Great Tang’s Dàhé era by the Bhikṣu Hǎiyún, a transmitter of the teachings at Jingzhù Monastery. Completed on the twenty-eighth day of the third month in the first year of Kuānxǐ. Transcribed by the Vajra-son Jìbiàn. It appears there are two or three different versions of this text.
On the final day of the eleventh month in the fifth year of Eiren (1297), the copying and collation of the above manuscript were completed.
Thus, with a heart moved by the Master’s name, I transcribed this while braving the cold snow and disregarding the freezing wind; Jishin records it here.
It was revised on the final day of the third month in the sixth year of Enbun (1361),
during the Kang’an era. On the seventh day of the fourth month,
it was transcribed from the original manuscript of the Venerable Jishin at Kanchiin in Tōji.
However, there are many erroneous characters which may be corrected directly.
This was completed on the twenty-ninth day of the month, having been transcribed from a manuscript and collated over ten days.
This record exists in variant editions.
Although it is included in the versions compiled by the Japanese masters Ennin, Enchō, Enchin, Son'e, and Henmyō,
it is not recorded in the present edition.
I suspect this may be the original root text.
Since this record was compiled in the eighth year of the Taishō era,
some years have already passed since the time he entered Tang China to study the Dharma, which occurred after the Taishō era.
How could one possibly record his name?
It is known that this was produced by later generations;
nevertheless, I have retained this original manuscript as it was transcribed.
